pl-l2d37c2-d1e108.summary: Objects to the former view: saying God is not author of evils insofar as evil, but insofar as they are, and that as evil they are nothing, is no wonder, since nothing has no author. So when God is called author of all that is, these understand goods, which exist naturally: not only substances and what is concreated, but all that does not deprive nature of good; Scripture's mentions of nature and substance must be read variously.
claims: God's authorship extends to all that does not deprive nature of good.

pl-l2d37c2-d1e111.summary: Cites Augustine on 'there is no substance' (Ps 68:3), seeming to agree: substance is what we are, man, beast, earth, sun; God made man a substance, but by iniquity man fell from it; iniquity is not a nature God formed but a perversion man made; in the hymn of the three youths all creation praises God, the serpent but not avarice, since vices come from our will and are not substance.

pl-l2d37c2-d1e116.summary: Urges those holding the former view to attend to these words to grasp what Scripture means by nature or substance.

pl-l2d37c2-d1e120.summary: Leaves the judgment between these views to the prudent reader, having given full knowledge of both, and hastens to remaining questions.

pl-l2d37c2-d1e123.summary: Notes all Catholics agree God is not author of evils, but evils must not include punishments, of which God is author: 'there is no evil in the city that the Lord has not done' (Amos 3:6) and 'I create evil and make good' (Isa 45:7), where evil means punishment, not sin.
claims: God is author of punishments, not sins.

pl-l2d37c2-d1e126.summary: Cites the Retractationes: 'God is not author of evil' must not be taken to mean the punishment of the wicked is not from him, which is evil to those punished; it was said as 'God did not make death,' though 'life and death are from the Lord'; punishment is evil to the wicked but among God's good works, since it is just. God did not make death in that he did not make sin, for which death is inflicted.

pl-l2d37c2-d1e131.summary: Concludes that the reader has the reason for saying God is not author of evil and did not make death.

pl-l2d37c2.summary: Objects to the first view: if God is not author of evils insofar as they are nothing, that is trivial, since nothing has no author. The second view takes 'author of all that is' to mean goods, those that exist naturally: substances, what is concreated, and all that does not deprive nature of good; Augustine on Ps 68 supports it: substance is what we are; iniquity is not substance but perversion made by man; all creation praises God in the hymn of the three youths, the serpent but not avarice, since vices come from our will. Lombard leaves the judgment between the two views to the prudent reader. All Catholics agree God is not author of evils, but 'evils' must not include punishments, which God makes ('I create evil,' Isa 45:7); Augustine clarifies that God is not author of evil means of sin, as 'God did not make death' means he did not make sin, for which death is inflicted, though punishment of the wicked is just and good.
claims: Saying God is not author of evil insofar as it is nothing would be trivial.
The second view restricts God's authorship to natures and what does not deprive nature of good.
Iniquity is not substance but a perversion made by man.
Lombard leaves the choice between the two views to the reader.
God is author of punishments but not of sins.
Punishment of the wicked is evil to them but good as just.
